Name: Phoebe Pettit
Badge: Teacher as Researcher | Sustaining Literacy Routines
Looking back on this inquiry cycle, what did you learn about your teaching and your students that you might not have noticed otherwise? How did engaging in this teacher-research process shape or shift your thinking about your classroom practice?:

Looking back on this inquiry cycle, I learned that my students are much more capable of engaging in complex thinking and writing when they are given the right supports and structure, like sentence stems, chunked texts, and collaborative discussion opportunities. I also noticed that small instructional shifts such as adding visuals, breaking down readings, or providing multiple entry points can make a big difference in student confidence and participation, especially for reluctant writers.

Engaging in this teacher research process really shifted my thinking about pacing and flexibility in the classroom. Instead of feeling tied to a single plan or product, I found myself more willing to adjust in the moment based on student response, which ultimately led to stronger engagement and higher-quality student work.

Think back to a moment during the lesson sequence that stands out. It could be a comment from a student, an unexpected challenge or success, a shift in engagement, or a moment when your own thinking changed. Describe what happened and why this moment feels meaningful to you now. What does it reveal:
What made it meaningful was the shift that happened after I broke the article into strips—students immediately re-engaged, started talking, and contributed to the conversation in ways they hadn’t before. It revealed how much the format of a task can impact student willingness to participate, and it reminded me that access is just as important as content when planning instruction.
As you look over the drafts your students produced in this lesson sequence, what early patterns, surprises, or questions are emerging for you? What aspects of your students’ writing are you most curious to explore more deeply with colleagues during our April regroup? What, if any, questions do you h:
As I look over student drafts, I’m noticing that students are more willing to share ideas than fully develop them in writing. Sentence stems and structure clearly help them get started, but many responses still need stronger evidence and explanation. I’m curious about how to better support students in moving from discussion to more independent argumentative writing. I’d also like to explore ways to build stronger reasoning without removing the supports too quickly.
